title: Ember Pulled Pork Baked Potatoes
summary: Giant baked potatoes stuffed with pulled pork, melted cheddar, BBQ sauce, sour cream, and green onions.
story: A baked potato is just a delivery vehicle, and pulled pork is the best cargo. Bake the potatoes until the skins crisp, fluff the insides, and load them up. This is a full meal in a potato.

items: Butter and salt for the potatoes

steps.title: Bake
steps.body: Rub potatoes with oil and salt. Bake at 400°F for 50–60 minutes until tender.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Split open, fluff with a fork, add butter. Pile on pulled pork and cheddar.

steps.title: Top
steps.body: Drizzle with BBQ sauce, dollop sour cream, and sprinkle green onions.

title: Ember Redneck Egg Rolls
summary: Crispy egg rolls stuffed with pulled pork, melty cheddar, and coleslaw — BBQ joint meets Chinese takeout, and it works.
story: Redneck egg rolls are a BBQ joint staple: pulled pork and slaw rolled up in an egg roll wrapper and fried golden. Crunchy outside, smoky and tangy inside. Dunk them in BBQ sauce.

steps.title: Fill
steps.body: Lay out a wrapper. Add ¼ cup pulled pork, 2 tablespoons coleslaw, and a pinch of shredded cheddar. Roll tight, sealing the edge with beaten egg.

steps.title: Fry
steps.body: Fry in 350°F oil for 3–4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden. Drain on a rack.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve hot with BBQ sauce for dipping.

title: Ember Witch's Brew Halloween Punch
summary: A blood-red party punch with floating gummy eyeballs and worms, fog rolling off dry ice — the kids go crazy for it.
story: Every Halloween party needs a centerpiece, and a smoking punch bowl is the easiest one there is. Cranberry and grape juice make it blood-red, lemon-lime soda keeps it fizzy, and sherbet scoops melt into it like something from a cauldron. The gummy eyeballs are what the kids remember. For the grown-ups: pour your own cup first, then add whatever alcohol you like.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: In a large punch bowl, stir together the cranberry juice, grape juice, and lemon-lime soda.

steps.title: Float
steps.body: Add scoops of orange sherbet and scatter in the gummy eyeballs and worms.

steps.title: Fog
steps.body: Using tongs, add dry ice around the OUTSIDE of the bowl or in a smaller bowl nested inside — never put dry ice directly in cups people drink from. The fog rolls for about 30 minutes; add more as needed.

steps.title: Adults
steps.body: Grown-ups can spike their own cups with vodka, rum, or whatever they like.

proTips: Chill everything first so the sherbet doesn't melt instantly.
Dry ice: tongs only, never touch with bare hands, and keep the room ventilated.

title: Ember Spiced Apple Punch (Warm or Cold)
summary: Good apple juice — not cider — simmered with cinnamon, cloves, star anise, orange, and ginger. Warm from the slow cooker or ice-cold over Sprite.
story: The app already has a smoked hot apple cider, so this one goes a different direction: quality apple juice instead of cider, which comes out clearer and lets the spices shine. Make it steaming in the slow cooker for a cold night, or chill it and pour it over ice with Sprite or ginger ale when it's warm out. The grown-ups get moonshine — apple pie moonshine in the warm cup, regular in the cold one.

items: 1 gallon quality apple juice (not from concentrate if you can find it)
Sprite or ginger ale, for the cold version
Apple pie moonshine or regular moonshine, for the adults

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Combine the apple juice, brown sugar, cinnamon sticks, cloves, star anise, orange slices, and ginger in a slow cooker or large pot.

steps.title: Warm version
steps.body: Slow cooker on low 2–3 hours until steaming and spiced through. Ladle into mugs.

steps.title: Cold version
steps.body: Simmer 20 minutes on the stove, chill, then serve over ice topped with Sprite or ginger ale.

steps.title: Adults
steps.body: Splash of apple pie moonshine in the warm cup, regular moonshine in the cold one.

proTips: Not-from-concentrate juice makes a real difference here.
Fish out the whole cloves before serving if kids are drinking it.

title: Ember Cold Smoked Cheddar
summary: Sharp cheddar kissed with apple wood smoke — rested 2 weeks until the smoke sinks in deep.
story: Cold smoking cheese is patience, not fire. Keep the chamber under 90 degrees, let apple wood do its work for a few hours, then wrap it up and forget it in the fridge for two weeks. What comes out the other side doesn't taste like the cheese you started with.

items: 1 block sharp cheddar (8 oz or larger)
Apple, cherry, or pecan pellets for the smoke tube

steps.title: Set up cold smoke
steps.body: Use a smoke tube filled with pellets, or a pan of ice above your heat source — the goal is smoke with the chamber under 90°F so the cheese never melts.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Set the cheddar block on the grate and cold smoke with apple wood for 2–3 hours, keeping the chamber under 90°F.

steps.title: Rest (don't skip)
steps.body: Wrap the cheese tight in plastic wrap or vacuum seal and refrigerate for 2 weeks. Fresh off the smoke it tastes harsh — the rest lets the smoke mellow and sink in. This is the step that makes it.

proTips: Smoke on a cool day or at night — anything over 90°F and the cheese sweats and melts.
Don't taste it right off the smoker and judge it. The 2-week rest is everything.

title: Ember Cold Smoked Pepper Jack
summary: Pepper jack over cherry wood — the smoke plays off the peppers. Made for burgers.
story: Pepper jack already has attitude. Cherry wood smoke on top of it, a two-week rest, and you've got a slicing cheese that makes a burger taste like it came off a competition rig.

items: 1 block pepper jack (8 oz or larger)
Apple, cherry, or pecan pellets for the smoke tube

title: Ember Cold Smoked Gouda
summary: A gouda wheel over pecan or apple smoke — creamy inside, deep amber outside.
story: Gouda's the sleeper pick for smoking. It's already buttery and smooth, and a few hours of pecan or apple smoke plus the two-week rest turns it into the cheese plate centerpiece.

items: Apple, cherry, or pecan pellets for the smoke tube

steps.title: Set up cold smoke
steps.body: Use a smoke tube filled with pellets, or a pan of ice above your heat source — the goal is smoke with the chamber under 90°F so the cheese never melts.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Set the gouda on the grate and cold smoke with pecan or apple wood for 2–4 hours, keeping the chamber under 90°F.

steps.title: Rest (don't skip)
steps.body: Wrap the cheese tight in plastic wrap or vacuum seal and refrigerate for 2 weeks. Fresh off the smoke it tastes harsh — the rest lets the smoke mellow and sink in. This is the step that makes it.

title: Ember Smoked Stone Crab Claws
summary: Florida's crown jewel kissed with light smoke — served chilled with classic mustard sauce.
story: Stone crab claws come pre-cooked from the dock, so this isn't a long cook — it's a gentle warm smoke that lays flavor on without touching the delicate meat. Mild wood only; hickory would bulldoze it. Season opens October 15, and the first claws of the season are the sweetest.

items: Old Bay or your favorite seafood seasoning, light dusting

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Dust the claws lightly with Old Bay or seafood seasoning.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 180–200°F for 30–45 minutes over alder or apple wood. You're warming and flavoring, not cooking — the claws are already cooked.

steps.title: Chill and serve
steps.body: Chill the claws, crack, and serve with mustard sauce (stir mayo, mustards, and lemon together).

proTips: Keep the wood mild — stone crab is sweet and delicate, strong smoke ruins it.
Don't over-smoke. 45 minutes max; you're seasoning, not barbecuing.

title: Ember Smoked Beef Short Ribs
summary: Three-bone plate ribs rubbed with Ember House Rub, smoked low until the bark's black and the meat probes like butter.
story: Beef short ribs are brisket on a stick — same rich beef, same low-and-slow patience, but on the bone. Get the big 3-bone plate ribs (the dino bones), not the little chuck ones. Rub them heavy, smoke them low over oak, and don't rush the wrap. When the probe slides in like warm butter, they're done.

items: 1 rack 3-bone plate short ribs, trimmed of hard fat and silver skin
Ember House Rub (or coarse salt, black pepper, and garlic powder)

steps.title: Rub
steps.body: Coat the ribs generously on all sides with Ember House Rub. Rest 30 minutes while the pit comes up.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over oak or hickory, bone-side down, for 8–10 hours.

steps.title: Wrap
steps.body: Once the bark is dark and set (around 165–170°F internal), wrap in butcher paper.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Pull when probe-tender — the probe slides in with no resistance, usually 203–208°F. Rest 1 hour before slicing between the bones.

proTips: Plate ribs, not chuck ribs — the 3-bone plate is twice as thick and twice as good.
Don't slice hot. The rest lets the juices settle back in.

title: Ember Smoked Au Gratin Potatoes
summary: Thin-sliced potatoes layered with cream, garlic, and cheddar in a cast iron skillet — finished on the smoker.
story: Au gratin is already comfort food royalty. Put the skillet on the smoker instead of the oven and the whole thing picks up a kiss of wood smoke that makes people ask what your secret is. Slice the potatoes thin and even — that's the whole trick. Everything else is just layering and patience.

items: 3 lbs russet or Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and sliced ⅛-inch thick
Fresh thyme leaves, for the top

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Butter a 12-inch cast iron skillet. Warm the cream, milk, garlic, salt, and pepper in a saucepan until steaming — don't boil.

steps.title: Layer
steps.body: Fan a layer of potato slices in the skillet, pour over some warm cream, sprinkle cheddar. Repeat until everything's used, ending with cream.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 350°F for about 90 minutes, uncovered, until the top is golden brown and a knife slides through the center with no resistance.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Top with the remaining cheddar and thyme, give it 10 more minutes to melt, then rest 15 minutes before serving.

proTips: Slice thin and even — a mandoline earns its keep here. Thick slices won't cook through.
Yukon Golds hold their shape better than russets if you like distinct layers.

title: Ember Soup Beans & Cornbread
summary: Pinto beans simmered low with country ham, onion, and beef stock — plus skillet cornbread for sopping.
story: This is the mountain supper. Soup beans aren't fancy and they aren't trying to be — they're creamy, smoky, salty-sweet from the country ham, and they demand cornbread alongside. Kelly's version adds onion and a splash of beef stock to the pot liquor, which is the kind of small thing that makes people ask for the recipe.

items: 1 lb dried pinto beans, soaked overnight
1 country ham hock (or 1 cup diced country ham)
Salt and black pepper to taste
¼ cup bacon grease or oil

steps.title: Simmer the beans
steps.body: Cover the soaked beans, ham hock, onion, and beef stock with water in a heavy pot. Bring to a boil, then drop to a low simmer for 2½–3 hours, until the beans are creamy and the hock is falling apart.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Pull the hock, shred the meat back into the pot, and season with salt and pepper. Country ham is salty — taste before you salt.

steps.title: Bake the cornbread
steps.body: Heat bacon grease in a cast iron skillet until smoking. Stir the cornbread batter just until combined, pour into the hot skillet, and bake at 425°F for 20–25 minutes until golden.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Ladle beans into bowls with plenty of pot liquor. Serve with a wedge of cornbread — crumble it right in if that's how your people do it.

proTips: Don't rush the beans — creamy takes time, and the pot liquor is the whole point.
Save the cornbread batter lumps out; overmixing makes it tough.

title: Ember Killed Lettuce
summary: Leaf lettuce wilted with screaming-hot bacon grease, topped with crumbled bacon and green onions.
story: Killed lettuce — some folks call it wilted lettuce — is mountain cooking at its most honest. You take fresh leaf lettuce, pour hot bacon grease over it until it just slumps, and eat it warm. It sounds strange until you've had it, and then it tastes like somebody's grandma's kitchen.

items: 1 large head leaf lettuce (or 2 bunches green onions' worth of tender greens), torn

steps.title: Crisp the bacon
steps.body: Cook the bacon in a skillet until crisp. Pull it out and crumble it, but leave every drop of grease in the pan.

steps.title: Heat the grease
steps.body: Get the bacon grease smoking hot — it should shimmer. Stir in the vinegar (it'll sizzle) and a pinch of salt and pepper.

steps.title: Kill it
steps.body: Put the lettuce and green onions in a big bowl. Pour the hot grease over the top and toss fast — the lettuce should wilt but not cook down to nothing.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Top with the crumbled bacon and eat it immediately, while it's still warm.

proTips: The grease has to be HOT — lukewarm grease just makes greasy salad.
Use tender leaf lettuce, not iceberg. It needs to wilt, not crunch.
